parts.title: Renting a flat in Brunswick

turns.text: Good morning, Northside Property, Kylie Brannigan speaking. How can I help you?
turns.speaker: agent

turns.text: Oh, hi. I'm ringing about a flat I saw on your website. It's a two-bedroom place in Brunswick.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Right, we've got a couple in Brunswick at the moment. Let me just take your details first, and then we'll work out which one it is. Can I have your name?
turns.speaker: agent

turns.text: Yeah, it's Josh Templeton.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: And could you spell the surname for me?
turns.speaker: agent

turns.say: Sure. It's Templeton. T, E, M, P, L, E, T, O, N.
turns.text: Sure. It's Templeton. T-E-M-P-L-E-T-O-N.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Thanks, Josh. And do you have the full address of the flat you're interested in?
turns.speaker: agent

turns.say: Yeah, it's 22 Wattle Road. That's W, A, T, T, L, E.
turns.text: Yeah, it's 22 Wattle Road. That's W-A-T-T-L-E.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Oh yes, that's a lovely one. It's actually just come back on the market, because the people who'd signed up for it had to pull out at the last minute.
turns.speaker: agent

turns.text: Lucky me. What floor is it on? The photos made it look quite high up.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: It's on the second floor... sorry, no, I'm thinking of the one next door. This one's on the third floor, and there's a lift, so you won't be carrying your shopping up the stairs.
turns.speaker: agent

turns.say: Good. Now, the ad said the rent was four hundred and sixty dollars a week. Is that still right?
turns.text: Good. Now, the ad said the rent was $460 a week. Is that still right?
turns.speaker: caller

turns.say: Ah, that was the old price, I'm afraid. The owner's put it up since then, so it's now four hundred and eighty-five dollars a week. That's still pretty reasonable for the area, though.
turns.text: Ah, that was the old price, I'm afraid. The owner's put it up since then, so it's now $485 a week. That's still pretty reasonable for the area, though.
turns.speaker: agent

turns.text: Okay. And does that cover any of the bills?
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Electricity and gas are up to you, so you'd set those up in your own name. But the owner pays the water bill, so that one's included in the rent.
turns.speaker: agent

turns.text: That's handy. Would it be possible to have a look at the flat this week?
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Let me check the diary. I could do Thursday at 4.45, if that suits.
turns.speaker: agent

turns.text: Ah, I don't finish work until five on Thursdays. Is anything later possible?
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Hmm, how about 5.30? That's the latest I can do, I'm afraid.
turns.speaker: agent

turns.text: 5.30 is perfect. Thursday at 5.30, then.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Great, I'll put you in the diary. Please bring some photo ID along with you.
turns.speaker: agent

turns.text: Will do. While I've got you, could you tell me a bit about the area? I've just moved down from Brisbane, so I don't really know Melbourne yet.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Of course. Transport's very good. The nearest tram stop is only about two minutes' walk from the building, and the tram gets you into the city in about 25 minutes. There's a train station too, and the train's quicker, around 15 minutes, but the station's a fair walk away.
turns.speaker: agent

turns.text: I'll probably take the tram, then. What about shopping?
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: There's a big supermarket on Sydney Road. It's right next to the bank, and opposite the library. And it's open until 10 pm every night, which is handy if you work late.
turns.speaker: agent

turns.text: Great. I like to keep fit, actually. Is there anywhere outdoors to exercise?
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Well, there's a park about five minutes' walk away. It's got tennis courts, and an outdoor swimming pool as well. There used to be a running track, but they've turned that into a playground.
turns.speaker: agent

turns.text: Sounds good. And is there a gym nearby?
turns.speaker: caller

turns.say: There's one right above the supermarket. A membership is forty-five dollars a month. Or if you'd rather not sign up, you can pay twelve dollars each time you go.
turns.text: There's one right above the supermarket. A membership is $45 a month. Or if you'd rather not sign up, you can pay $12 each time you go.
turns.speaker: agent

turns.say: forty-five dollars a month isn't bad at all. Anything else worth knowing about?
turns.text: $45 a month isn't bad at all. Anything else worth knowing about?
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: There's a farmers' market in the grounds of the primary school. It used to run on Saturdays, but it's moved to Sunday mornings now. Lots of fresh fruit and veg, and great coffee.
turns.speaker: agent

turns.text: I'll definitely check that out. Oh, one last thing. Is there a garage? I've got a car.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: No garage, unfortunately. But you can park on the street outside the building. You just need a resident permit from the council. It's free, you only have to fill in a form online.
turns.speaker: agent

turns.text: That's fine. Thanks so much, Kylie. See you on Thursday.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: See you then, Josh. Just give me a ring on this number if anything changes.
turns.speaker: agent

parts.title: A reopened science museum

turns.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Ashbury Science Museum. My name's Owen Ratcliffe, and I'm one of the guides here. As you probably know, we've been closed for nearly two years, well, twenty-two months to be exact, while the building was renovated, so it's lovely to see visitors again. I'll start with the ground floor, and then I'll tell you about the new galleries upstairs.
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: Right, you've all got a copy of the ground-floor plan, I hope. We're standing just inside the main entrance, facing north. On your left is the ticket desk, and on your right is the shop.
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: Now, most of you will want somewhere to leave coats and bags. The room beside the ticket desk, to the west, looks as if it might be the cloakroom, but it's actually staff offices. The cloakroom's on the other side, right next to the shop, just beyond it to the east.
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: Then, if you walk straight up the main corridor, you'll come to a crossroads where it meets the long corridor running east to west. Just before that crossroads, there are two large rooms facing each other. The one on your left is the Energy Zone, which, I'm sorry to say, won't open until the summer. The one on your right is the Flight Gallery, with the old biplane hanging from the ceiling, and that's open now.
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: OK. At the crossroads, turn left and walk west, right to the end of the corridor. The room on your left, at the very end, is where we'll hold our temporary exhibitions. The first one's about volcanoes, and it's well worth a look. It runs until the end of September, and there's no extra charge for it.
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: Directly opposite it, on the right-hand side, is the picnic room. If you've brought your own sandwiches, that's the place to eat them. Please don't eat them in the café, which is just north of the picnic room. The café staff get rather upset about that!
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: Now, for families with small children. The play area used to be in the basement, but we've moved it up here. It's the long, narrow room between the café and the lifts. The lifts are at the far end of the main corridor, by the way, so if you're pushing a buggy, that's the easiest way to reach it.
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: And finally, the toilets. Go back to the crossroads, and this time follow the long corridor east instead of west. Right at the end, the door on your right is the toilets. Opposite them, on your left, is the lecture theatre, where there are free talks every afternoon.
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: Right, that's the ground floor. Now for the exciting part: the six brand-new galleries on the first floor. Every one of them has something hands-on, so let me quickly tell you what you can actually do in each.
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: Let's start with the Space Gallery. People always ask me if there's a telescope they can look through. I'm afraid there isn't; there simply wasn't room. But you can climb into a full-size copy of a space capsule, and with the screens and controls inside, it feels as if you're really docking with the space station.
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: Next door is the Medicine Gallery. Most of it's glass cases, as you'd expect, but there's a table in the middle where you can put on gloves and pick up genuine surgical tools from the 1800s. They're surprisingly heavy.
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: Then there's the Engineering Hall. You'll see a big robot arm in there, and children always want a go with it, but it's behind glass, so nobody can operate it, I'm afraid. What you can do is put together a little bridge out of card and straws, and then add weights to find out how much it'll hold before it falls down.
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: The Sound Studio is great fun, and it's especially popular with teenagers. There's a booth where you talk into a microphone, and it keeps a copy of what you've said so you can listen to yourself afterwards. Most people are shocked by what they sound like!
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: On the Chemistry Stage, you can't touch anything, for obvious safety reasons. But at 11 am, 1 pm and 3 pm each day, one of our scientists mixes chemicals in front of the audience, and you can watch the colours change and the smoke appear.
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: And last of all, the Climate Gallery. Along one wall there are touch screens with ten questions about the weather and the planet, and at the end, it tells you how many you got right. See if you can beat your children's score! Right, any questions before we head upstairs?
turns.speaker: guide

questions.prompt: Cloakroom
questions.evidence: The cloakroom's on the other side, right next to the shop, just beyond it to the east.

explanation.en: The cloakroom is just east of the shop. The room beside the ticket desk looks like it, but the guide says it is staff offices.
explanation.ru: "Cloakroom" находится сразу к востоку от магазина. Комната рядом с кассой похожа на него, но гид говорит, что там "staff offices", то есть служебные помещения.
explanation.uk: "Cloakroom" розташований одразу на схід від магазину. Кімната біля каси схожа на нього, але гід каже, що там "staff offices", тобто службові приміщення.

questions.prompt: Flight Gallery
questions.evidence: The one on your right is the Flight Gallery, with the old biplane hanging from the ceiling

explanation.en: Walking north up the main corridor, the Flight Gallery is on the right just before the crossroads. The room opposite it on the left is the Energy Zone.
explanation.ru: Если идти на север по главному коридору, "Flight Gallery" будет справа, прямо перед перекрёстком. Комната напротив, слева, это "Energy Zone".
explanation.uk: Якщо йти на північ головним коридором, "Flight Gallery" буде праворуч, перед самим перехрестям. Кімната навпроти, ліворуч, це "Energy Zone".

questions.prompt: Temporary exhibitions
questions.evidence: The room on your left, at the very end, is where we'll hold our temporary exhibitions.

explanation.en: Walking west along the long corridor, the temporary exhibitions room is on the left at the very end, not the first room on the left (the Energy Zone).
explanation.ru: Если идти на запад по длинному коридору, зал "temporary exhibitions" будет слева в самом конце. Это не первая комната слева: там "Energy Zone".
explanation.uk: Якщо йти на захід довгим коридором, зала "temporary exhibitions" буде ліворуч у самому кінці. Це не перша кімната ліворуч: там "Energy Zone".

questions.prompt: Picnic room
questions.evidence: Directly opposite it, on the right-hand side, is the picnic room.

explanation.en: The picnic room is opposite the temporary exhibitions room, on the right as you walk west, and just south of the café.
explanation.ru: "Picnic room" находится напротив зала "temporary exhibitions", справа, если идти на запад, и сразу к югу от кафе.
explanation.uk: "Picnic room" розташована навпроти зали "temporary exhibitions", праворуч, якщо йти на захід, і одразу на південь від кафе.

questions.prompt: Children's play area
questions.evidence: It's the long, narrow room between the café and the lifts.

explanation.en: The play area is the long, narrow room between the café and the lifts. It used to be in the basement, but it is now on the ground floor.
explanation.ru: "Play area" — это длинная узкая комната между кафе и лифтами. Раньше она была в подвале, но теперь находится на первом этаже.
explanation.uk: "Play area" — це довга вузька кімната між кафе та ліфтами. Раніше вона була в підвалі, але тепер розташована на першому поверсі.

segments.text: Part 3. You will hear two psychology students discussing how to collect data for a research project on exam stress. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24.
That is the end of Part 3. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers.

parts.title: Choosing a research method

turns.text: Hi Jordan. Okay, so Professor Reyes wants our method proposal by Friday, and we still haven't picked between interviews and a questionnaire. We really need to decide today.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Yeah, I know. I've been going back and forth on it. What's your feeling?
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Honestly, I keep coming back to interviews. Everyone says they give you richer, more detailed data, and that's true. But for me the big thing is that you can follow up. If someone says they just deal with stress, you can ask them to explain what they actually mean.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Right. And people probably feel more relaxed chatting than filling in a form, too.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Hmm, I'm not so sure about that, actually. A lot of students would find it pretty awkward talking to a stranger about stress. Anyway, what about you? You were leaning toward a questionnaire, weren't you?
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: I was. I mean, obviously you can reach way more people, and the results are a lot easier to analyze. But what really convinces me is that nobody has to give their name. With a topic like exam stress, people might not admit how badly they're coping if they're sitting across from you.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: That's a fair point. And there's the time issue. Remember what Professor Reyes said in class on Tuesday? I was half expecting her to tell us our topic was too broad, but she didn't. What she did say was that transcribing and coding interviews always takes about three times longer than students plan for.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Yeah, I remember that. Though I read somewhere that online surveys get really low response rates, so questionnaires aren't exactly a quick fix either.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: True. So what if we did both? A questionnaire first, and then interviews with five or six people afterward?
turns.speaker: student_a

parts.title: How migrating birds navigate

turns.text: Good morning, everyone. Today we're carrying on with animal behaviour, and I want to look at one of the big puzzles in zoology: how migrating birds find their way. Think of the bar-tailed godwit. Every September it leaves Alaska and flies non-stop to places like the Firth of Thames, here in New Zealand, a journey of over eleven thousand kilometres. So how on earth does it know where it's going?
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Let's start with the sun. In the 1950s a German scientist, Gustav Kramer, noticed something odd about caged starlings. When the season for migrating came round, they didn't sit still. They fluttered and hopped about, and they kept facing the direction they'd normally fly in. This is what we now call migratory restlessness, and it gave researchers a really handy way to measure which way a bird wants to go.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Kramer then asked whether the birds were actually using the sun. He thought about moving the cage, or putting lamps around it, but in the end he went for something simpler. He used mirrors to make the sun appear to be in a different position. And sure enough, the starlings turned to face a new direction, by just about the same amount he'd shifted the sun.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Now, there's a complication here. The sun moves across the sky during the day, so a bird can't just fly towards it. It has to adjust for the time, and to do that it needs an internal clock. Researchers showed this by keeping birds under artificial lights that were switched on six hours late. Their clocks were thrown out, and they headed off in the wrong direction, just as you'd predict.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: But lots of birds migrate at night. So what about the stars? In the 1960s an American researcher, Stephen Emlen, studied a small songbird called the indigo bunting. People often assume he took them to an observatory, but no, he tested them inside a planetarium, where he could control exactly which stars they saw.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: What he found was fascinating. Young buntings don't come with a star map built in. Instead, as they grow, they learn which part of the sky the stars turn around, the centre of rotation, which in the northern hemisphere is close to the Pole Star. And when Emlen made the planetarium sky rotate around a different star, the birds treated that star as north.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Right, the third cue is the earth's magnetic field. In the 1960s Wolfgang Wiltschko put European robins in cages surrounded by electric coils, which let him change the magnetic field. The robins changed direction too. But here's the surprising part. Robins don't sense whether the field points north or south, the way a compass needle does. What they detect is the angle of the field lines in relation to the ground.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: So where's the sensor? For a long time people thought it was tiny bits of iron in the beak. That idea hasn't really held up, I'm afraid. The current theory is that it involves light-sensitive proteins in the eye, which may mean that birds can actually see the magnetic field in some way.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: There's a nice example of how sensitive this system is. A team in Oldenburg, in Germany, found their robins couldn't orient at all in wooden huts on the university campus. The cause turned out to be weak electrical noise from equipment around the city. Once the huts were lined with aluminium and grounded, the birds oriented perfectly again.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: OK. Those three compasses get a bird into the right general area. But near the end of a journey, many birds switch to what they can see. They pick up familiar landmarks, things like coastlines, rivers and mountain ranges, much as you would on a road trip down the South Island.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Homing pigeons give us good evidence for this. Researchers at Oxford fitted pigeons with GPS trackers and found they flew along the same routes again and again. I'd expected them to follow railway lines, which are straight and easy to see, but in fact the birds mostly followed major roads, even turning at junctions.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Finally, smell, which was the most controversial idea. In Italy in the 1970s, Floriano Papi worked with pigeons that had lost their sense of smell. Near their loft they were fine. But when they were released at unfamiliar sites, a long way off, most of them never made it home.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Plenty of scientists doubted this, partly because birds were thought to have a weak sense of smell. Then, in 2015, a study looked at Scopoli's shearwaters, which are seabirds. Some had their sense of smell blocked for a short time. Over open ocean they got lost, but they could still navigate when they were flying along the coast, where they could use what they saw.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: So what's the overall picture? Birds don't rely on a single system. They combine several, and switch between them depending on the weather and where they are. That's why they're so reliable.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: For next week, I'd like you to read about a newer problem. We used to worry mainly about noise from cities, but the bigger threat to night-flying birds seems to be light pollution, which can draw them off course. We'll look at what can be done about it. Thanks, everyone.
turns.speaker: lecturer
